item.title: Fort Hood Shooter’s Execution Will be Public and Streamed Live, Pentagon Says
item.description:
Pentagon officials said on Thursday that the Army officer convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting would be executed in public, a practice that ended in the United States nearly a century ago and is most commonly carried out in a handful of countries including Iran, North Korea and the Taliban-led government in Afghanistan.

The Pentagon said in a statement that the military execution, scheduled for Dec. 3, would also be broadcast via livestream. Such a broadcast has little precedent, and releasing video of executions is most often associated with extremist militant groups like the Islamic State.

The announcement adds to the growing spectacle around the planned execution of Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people and wounded 32 others when he brought a personal handgun onto the grounds of Fort Hood, Texas. The rampage was the deadliest shooting at an American military base and sent shock waves through the U.S. military.

There are few countries that hold public executions. The human rights group Amnesty International has highlighted some cases in which public executions in Iran and Saudi Arabia have been filmed by bystanders.

The practice of filming and releasing video of an execution is more common with terror groups like the Islamic State, which became infamous for videos of gruesome executions of prisoners who were not given due process or convicted of crimes. Mass shooters have in some cases broadcast their killing sprees on livestream sites.

In an interview with Real America’s Voice, a conservative outlet, aboard the aircraft carrier U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said Thursday that the execution would be public and available to watch “because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.” The Pentagon later confirmed in a statement that the execution would be livestreamed.

The Army has said the public execution of Major Hasan will be conducted by firing squad at Fort Hood, the site of the shooting. If carried out, it would be a first in modern American history.

The last state-sanctioned public execution in the United States occurred more than 90 years ago in Owensboro, Kentucky. Some 20,000 people gathered to witness the August 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea, a young Black man who had been convicted of raping an elderly white woman.

Major Hasan’s execution would be the first by the military justice system since 1961, and he would be the first soldier put to death by firing squad since World War II. The firing squad is a rare method of execution, but one that has been used by the military, particularly during wartime. The Trump administration has proposed expanding its use as a method of execution.

Mr. Hegseth said that the decision to shoot Major Hasan by a firing squad, as well as other details of the execution, were chosen for their symbolism.

“Of course we’re going to do it at Fort Hood,” Mr. Hegseth said. “And do it on a Thursday and we’re going to do it at 1 o’clock — which is when he did it — and it’s going to be soldiers with rifles executing the firing squad. It hadn’t been since World War II since we’ve done that.”

He continued, “Well I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II.”

On Nov. 5, 2009, Major Hasan, an Army psychiatrist stationed at Fort Hood, brought a personal handgun onto the base grounds and opened fire. Major Hasan said that he carried out the attack, which occurred at the height of the post-9/11 fight against terrorism, to wage jihad for what he called the illegal and immoral wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. He admitted to the killings during his court-martial and was convicted in 2013 of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder.

Major Hasan, who was wounded in the shooting, is being held at the military death row prison in Fort Leavenworth, Kan. He expressed no remorse for his actions, and told a military mental health panel that he wished he had died in the attack so that he could have become a martyr.

Mr. Hegseth and other Pentagon officials emphasized Major Hasan’s motivations for the shooting in their public statements about the execution. Mr. Hegseth also criticized President Barack Obama for not describing the attack at the time as an act of terror.

Speaking at a rally in Texas on Wednesday, Mr. Trump, a vocal advocate of the death penalty, trumpeted his order to execute Major Hasan, telling the crowd in San Antonio that “we are going to deliver final justice to an evil killer.”

item.title: 5 Key Moments From a Hostile Michigan Debate: ‘You Going After My Mom?’
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, and former Representative Mike Rogers, his Republican rival, spent most of their first televised debate rushing to unload a campaign’s worth of attack lines and opposition research.

Family members were invoked. Insinuations about ties to terrorists were made. Accusations of corruption abounded. And here and there, policy was discussed.

The debate comes as both candidates wrestle for a foothold among swing voters, with polls showing a tight race. The contest could be critical for determining Senate control and has been among the most expensive in the country. A second and final debate is scheduled for Oct. 21 in Detroit.

Here are five key moments from the debate:

Perhaps the most contentious moment came during an exchange over Flock Safety cameras, which Dr. El-Sayed said should be regulated by the federal government.

Mr. Rogers said the cameras were useful for catching people suspected of being terrorists. “Why would that bother you?” he seemed to wonder aloud. “Well, if you have someone in your family that might be on the, on the watch list …”

Dr. El-Sayed, who is of Egyptian descent and would become the country’s first Muslim senator if elected — and who has faced racist and Islamophobic attacks on the campaign trail — seemed to suggest in his response that Mr. Rogers was accusing him of being tied to terrorism.

“Go ahead and say it,” Dr. El Sayed said. “You’ve been tiptoeing around it the whole time.”

Throughout the debate, Mr. Rogers had repeatedly brought up terrorist groups like Al Qaeda and Hamas, suggesting that Dr. El-Sayed was supported by people who backed such organizations. Dr. El-Sayed either ignored or parried the claims, and his campaign denied them, pointing to articles that said they were false or misleading.

Dr. El-Sayed is a fierce critic of Israel, Mr. Rogers is a staunch supporter, and the issue has loomed over the race in Michigan, which has many Jewish and Arab American voters.

Mr. Rogers initially declined to say whether there was “any action by the Israeli government” that would cause him to oppose U.S. military aid for the country, calling it a “pretty hypothetical question.” Then he said American support for Israel was a matter of U.S. national security.

Pressed again, Mr. Rogers said Israel would lose his support if the country was “talking about using nuclear weapons.”

Dr. El-Sayed, for his part, refused to answer a question about whether Iran or Israel was a greater threat to the U.S., calling it “a ridiculous hypothetical.”

“I think both of them have proven dangerous in their own way,” Dr. El-Sayed said when asked again, after saying Israel was responsible for pushing the U.S. into the Iran war. “One at risk of attacking us, one getting us into wars we have no business fighting.”

The candidates also traded blows over artificial intelligence.

Mr. Rogers said local governments needed to determine whether data centers that power A.I. should be built in their communities. He has backed a temporary pause on data center construction, but he expressed hesitancy about federal regulations on them.

Dr. El-Sayed has not backed such a moratorium, though he supports strong federal guardrails for data centers.

On artificial intelligence, Dr. El-Sayed defended his proposal to put A.I. companies under public control. He has said that more than half of board members at leading A.I. companies should be publicly appointed or democratically elected, rather than chosen by shareholders.

“If the corporations and their C.E.O.s are right that this is going to take nearly 50 percent of our white-collar jobs, I think it’s important for the public to have a real stake,” he said.

The candidates attacked each other at every opportunity, with jabs about Mr. Rogers’s Florida property, Dr. El-Sayed’s medical credentials and much more.

One moment epitomized this.

“Let’s do this. Let’s — let’s open up this can of worms,” Mr. Rogers said in the middle of their heated exchange about terrorism. He then started to talk pointedly about his own mother, and went on to make a dark insinuation about Dr. El-Sayed’s mother’s ties to groups working in the Middle East.

Dr. El-Sayed responded, “You going after my mom?”

One comment from the moderator, Rick Albin, a local political reporter, encapsulated the animosity: The candidates were still needling each other out of sight of TV viewers.

“I want to take a quick aside and tell you that in 30 years of doing debates, I’ve never seen it continue during the commercial,” the exasperated moderator said. “But it did.”

item.title: Fiery Senate Debates in Maine, Michigan and Georgia: Five Takeaways
item.description:
A trio of debates in key Senate races on Thursday night underscored how fraught the midterms have become, as candidates in Maine, Michigan and Georgia traded personal and heated attacks.

In Michigan, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, said former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, was a warmonger, while Mr. Rogers tried to tie Dr. El-Sayed, a Muslim, to terrorism.

In Georgia, Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, called Representative Mike Collins, a Republican, a “bigot.”

And in Maine, Senator Susan Collins demanded a public apology after her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, accused her and her husband of profiting from the Iran war.

Here are five takeaways from the debates across three states that could determine control of the Senate.

In all three debates, Democrats said that Republicans marched in lock step with the unpopular president.

Again and again, Mr. Jackson charged Ms. Collins with failing to use her power to oppose Trump administration policies that have hurt Maine, including the war in Iran and tariffs. “We are in a crisis now,” he said of energy prices, “because she and her Republican colleagues would not stand up to Donald Trump.”

In Georgia, Mr. Ossoff asked Mr. Collins repeatedly how President Trump’s tariffs have helped Georgians, at one point calling them the “Mike Collins-Donald Trump tariffs.” Mr. Ossoff argued that economic pain for farmers and increased health care premiums for consumers were both “predictable,” but Mr. Collins still voted for Trump-backed policies that contributed to them.

“Whatever Donald Trump says, Mike Collins does,” Mr. Ossoff said. “Doesn’t matter what it is. Doesn’t think for himself.”

And in Michigan, Dr. El-Sayed accused Mr. Rogers of being “a guy who wants to be a sock puppet for the Trump administration,” especially over the war in Iran, which has pushed gasoline prices higher.

You can usually tell who is winning debates based on the questions. Candidates on offense get to talk about issues that are good for them, while those on defense are trying to change the subject to more favorable territory.

The problem for the Republican candidates in Thursday’s debates — along with their compatriots running for offices across the country — is that the issues core to voters’ concerns this year are not good for them. Moderators asked about high gas prices, Mr. Trump’s tariffs, the Iran war and immigration raids — all topics that forced Republicans to defend unpopular Trump administration policies or explain why they are now skeptical of stances they previously supported.

There were no questions across the three debates about transgender athletes in youth sports, a topic that often divides Democrats and that Mr. Trump and the super PACs he controls have used to attack Democratic candidates.

In the Michigan debate, Dr. El-Sayed was not asked about his association with Hasan Piker, the left-wing streamer who campaigned with him during the primary but has since kept his distance. In Maine, Mr. Jackson was not asked whether he is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, which has endorsed his bid and backed his run for governor earlier this year.

It took just 20 seconds into his first answer, about the federal gas tax, for Dr. El-Sayed to attack Mr. Rogers for backing the war in Iran.

There would not be a single exchange during the debate that did not include a personal attack, with the two men frequently interrupting each other. The two argued about second homes — Mr. Rogers’s in Florida and Dr. El-Sayed’s overseas. Dr. El-Sayed, who was quicker on his feet and a smoother talker, got the best of Mr. Rogers on many of these exchanges, frustrating the former congressman.

Their jousting continued when they were off the air.

“In 30 years of doing debates, I’ve never seen it continue during the commercial, but it did,” said the moderator, Rick Ablin, of the Grand Rapids NBC affiliate.

Perhaps the nastiest, most personal exchanges came when Mr. Rogers tried to tie Dr. El-Sayed to terror organizations. He said the man running to be the first Muslim in the Senate is “bought off by Hamas, Hezbollah, Al Qaeda, those people who are supporting you, pour that money into your campaign.”

There is no evidence Dr. El-Sayed has support from terror groups.

When he got a chance to speak uninterrupted, he called Mr. Rogers desperate.

“He wants this to be about anything but his own record,” Dr. El-Sayed said.

Mr. Ossoff began the Georgia Senate debate saying it would be the “trial of Mike Collins.” Then, he set out to prosecute his case.

He accused the Republican congressman of hiring “half the Third Reich,” referring to past Collins aides who have espoused white nationalist and antisemitic views. He slammed him for reposting a video in 2024 of white male students taunting and jeering a female Black student with racist and profane remarks.

“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery,” Mr. Ossoff said, “Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club.”

Mr. Collins said that he has “condemned racism, antisemitism, hate.” And he tried to turn the tables on Mr. Ossoff, who is Jewish, by criticizing the Democrat’s support for Dr. El-Sayed, whom Mr. Collins claimed “hates Israel” and “loves Iran.”

Mr. Ossoff, who is the more polished debater, tied every policy problem to Mr. Trump, while Mr. Collins, who owns a trucking company, leaned into his experience to suggest he was more in touch with regular Georgians.

Mr. Jackson shifted his approach for the second Maine Senate debate of the week. He devoted far less attention to questioning Ms. Collins’s support for abortion rights and her vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who joined the conservative Supreme Court majority that overturned Roe v. Wade. Instead, he honed his attacks on rising costs, including the drastic increase in heating oil prices, and accusations that Ms. Collins is abusing her position for personal gain.

“Ever since I was a young boy, I watched power and corruption hold people back,” Mr. Jackson said of reports that the F.B.I. last year shut down an inquiry into corruption allegations against an adviser to Ms. Collins.

That prompted a sharp response from Ms. Collins. She repeatedly charged Mr. Jackson — whom she called “Troy” throughout the debate — with lying about her record. “These allegations are absolutely false, and they’ve been proven false.” She also accused Mr. Jackson of running “false ads” about the issue.

item.title: The Controversial Class That M.I.T. Is Paying a Professor Not to Teach
item.description:
The name of the proposed Massachusetts Institute of Technology course was as provocative as it was long:

“Language and Linguistics for Decolonization and Liberation and for Peace and Community Building — From the River to the Sea in Palestine and Israel to the Mountaintops of Haiti and Beyond.”

The instructor was Michel DeGraff, a longtime tenured linguistics professor at M.I.T. who came up with the idea in the months after the Oct. 7 Hamas attack on Israel. He was a leading faculty voice siding with pro-Palestinian campus protesters, whose frequent rallying cry for Palestinian freedom, “from the river to the sea,” was seen by some Jews as antisemitic.

An M.I.T. panel rejected the course over questions about whether Dr. DeGraff, a Haitian scholar and expert in the study of Creole languages, had the expertise to teach it. That was supposed to finish the matter.

To Dr. DeGraff, it was more like the starting gun.

He disagreed that he lacked the ability to teach the course and protested the decision in a flurry of emails decrying it as part of a “new McCarthyism.” He complained to his colleagues, including deans and the university’s president in long email chains — which he then made public.

He objected on social media and in published commentaries. He filed a federal lawsuit against M.I.T., accusing the school of chilling campus speech on Gaza and violating his academic freedom.

“M.I.T. should not be repressing my teaching in this way,” Dr. DeGraff said in an interview. He called the decision a “violation of my professional rights.”

The university, though a spokeswoman, declined to comment, though it has denied Dr. DeGraff’s claims in legal filings.

As Dr. DeGraff’s profile has risen, so has the volume of his critics. He was sued for harassment by a Jewish former student. A U.S. House committee staff report last spring accused him of perpetuating “antisemitic conspiracy theories.”

Now three years into the dispute, his personal relationship with the M.I.T. linguistics section head, a onetime friend, is broken, and colleagues are exhausted by the controversy.

In many other American workplaces, employees who push back so forcefully would most likely risk their employment. But tenured professors are, by design, hard to get rid of.

Administrators have sanctioned Dr. DeGraff, accusing him of being disruptive and violating procedures and directives. He was pushed out of M.I.T.’s linguistics section and given the nebulous title of “faculty at large,” which he includes in his email signature inside satirical quotation marks.

He said in an interview that he had been denied a scheduled raise and access to new mentees, and had even been blocked from the department’s Facebook page. For the third fall semester in a row, he said, he is being paid while not teaching a class.

He is one of a number of professors in disputes with their schools over speech recently.

Carnegie Mellon University announced in September that it was investigating social media posts from a professor who is accused of celebrating the deaths of conservative figures.

A University of Texas professor is contesting his 16-month paid administrative leave, which he believes is related to his criticism of school leadership.

And an arbitrator ordered San Jose State University to reinstate a tenured professor the university had fired over allegations related to her role in pro-Palestinian campus protests.

At a time when campus politics are under a microscope and schools are trying to avoid the attention of the Trump administration, Dr. DeGraff’s fight has become one of the longest and most dramatic.

Chris Sharp, chief of staff at the Cicero Institute, a public policy organization based in Austin, said some tenured professors were cloaking their personal activism under the guise of “academic freedom.” The term, he said, is often misconstrued as the right to teach or research without limit, when it should be understood as the right to teach and research within one’s specialty.

“Just because I have a Ph.D. in one thing does not make me an expert in everything,” he said.

Friends of Dr. DeGraff say his campaign for his proposed class came from his deep concern for free speech, human rights and his understanding of language as a means to exercise power.

“Michel’s great virtue is his persistence,” said Haynes Miller, an M.I.T. professor emeritus of mathematics who is close to Dr. DeGraff and who says his friend is not an antisemite. “He doesn’t give up. If he sees an injustice he will attack it.”

Dr. DeGraff, 63, was born in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, and persuaded his parents to send him to the United States to study computer science. But once there, he became more interested in his homeland’s language, Haitian Creole, which, he said, is often derided as “broken French” and not a real language.

His Ph.D. thesis at the University of Pennsylvania was entitled “Creole Grammars and Acquisition of Syntax: The Case of Haitian Creole,” he said. He joined the M.I.T. linguistics faculty in 1996.

Dr. DeGraff sees parallels between the Haitian struggle for independence and that of Palestinian people. “That is what brought me to want to further my research and teaching about these connections,” he said.

The idea for the class came to him on Dec. 5, 2023, after he had watched M.I.T.’s president, Sally Kornbluth, and leaders of Harvard and the University of Pennsylvania get rhetorically beat up by Republicans in a congressional hearing on campus antisemitism.

After the course was rejected, he turned the concept into a discussion series with guest speakers in the fall of 2024.

That year, he also frequently joined students who occupied part of campus in a three-week encampment demanding that the school end ties with Israel. He was there nearly every day, he said, before the police shut it down.

Agustín Rayo, dean of the M.I.T. School of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences, sanctioned Dr. DeGraff in late 2024. In a letter Dr. DeGraff shared, the dean said he was removing Dr. DeGraff temporarily from the linguistics section for being disruptive and creating the expectation that people who displease him “are at risk of being targeted” in public forums.

“Your speech rights do not place you above M.I.T.’s rules,” the dean wrote in the letter.

Dr. DeGraff also came to the attention of congressional Republicans, who in a report pointed to accusations that Dr. DeGraff had targeted a Jewish student for harassment. That former student, William Sussman, joined a lawsuit against Dr. DeGraff and the school in 2025.

Mr. Sussman said Dr. DeGraff targeted him on social media as an example of a Zionist “mind infection” for his pro-Israel views. Mr. Sussman has said antisemitic harassment drove him out of the university.

Dr. DeGraff said the term “mind infection” came from an Israeli scholar who has used it to refer to how Israeli schoolbooks marginalize Palestinians. Dr. DeGraff said he was not an antisemite and that federal courts had said that criticism of Israel by itself is not inherently antisemitic.

Part of the suit, including the claims against Dr. DeGraff, was dismissed, though appeals are possible.

In a statement, Mr. Sussman criticized M.I.T., saying “the professor remains employed at M.I.T., where he continues to smear me.”

His removal from the linguistics department means “his impact at M.I.T. is substantially reduced,” said Dr. Miller, the friend of Dr. DeGraff’s. “It is humiliating for him; it’s a symbolic thing as well as a practical thing.”

Last March, Dr. DeGraff filed a federal lawsuit against M.I.T., along with the congressional committee that had named him in its report and its chairman. In his suit, he accuses the university of punishing him for his political activism.

“If you ask faculty to keep quiet, then you are basically betraying the job of the university, which is to teach about difficult topics,” he said.

M.I.T. denied his claims and asked the court to dismiss the suit.

“Indeed, the fact that DeGraff has continued to speak publicly and prolifically on the very subjects he claims have been chilled only underscores the speculative nature of his alleged injuries,” the university argued in a court filing.

He is still scheduled to teach the spring classes he has taught for years, “Creole Languages and Caribbean Identities” and “Black Matters: Introduction to Black Studies.”

Over this past summer, Dr. DeGraff proposed another new course, based on his book, published last month: “Our Own Language: Harnessing the Power of Kreyol and Other Mother Tongues for Education and Liberation.”

It is common for professors at a research university such as M.I.T. to propose new courses. And in early September, an associate dean told Dr. DeGraff the department would discuss the idea. But first, could he provide a copy of the book?

No, Dr. DeGraff replied, the syllabus he submitted should be enough. Given the history with his last course proposal, he wrote, “requiring an additional departmental review of the book itself therefore strikes me as ongoing discrimination and harassment.” He looped in top administrators, including Dr. Kornbluth, to his email.

His new class, he said, was rejected.

item.title: How Trump’s Revenge Campaign Descended Into Turmoil
item.description:
Joseph diGenova, the man assigned by the White House to lead the investigation into those who investigated President Trump, was walking out of Chuck’s Seafood near the beach in Fort Pierce, Fla., and toward his Tesla last month when his cellphone buzzed.

It was his boss, Attorney General Todd Blanche. And he was spluttering mad.

Mr. Blanche had been cautiously supportive of Mr. Trump’s decision to call Mr. diGenova, 81, out of retirement in April to kick-start the so-called grand conspiracy case, the Justice Department’s most expansive effort to pursue people the president considers his enemies.

Now the attorney general, having soured on Mr. diGenova, was livid that he had lashed out at two prosecutors sent from Washington to help move the case along. Mr. Blanche ordered him to his office on Sept. 11 — or else, according to people briefed on the exchange.

Assuming he would be fired, Mr. diGenova quit, dealing the latest blow to a troubled investigation central to the president’s vengeance agenda. More trouble was to come.

Soon after, a top diGenova deputy, Kurt Olsen, also quit. It turned out he had failed a polygraph test about his contacts with foreigners, which imperiled his security clearance, according to two people familiar with the matter. Mr. Olsen said he complied with all requirements regarding foreign contacts and had not resigned over his clearance, but declined to say more.

Still, the dual departures laid bare months of dysfunction. They also offered fresh evidence that Mr. Trump’s demands for revenge have divided the Justice Department, diverted resources from other investigations and continued the erosion of the principle that politics must be kept strictly separate from federal law enforcement.

A New York Times examination of the inquiry, based on more than 20 interviews with current and former officials, found that it was star-crossed from the outset.

The theory of the grand conspiracy case is a bedrock of Trumpist politics: that the various investigations into Mr. Trump, spanning nearly a decade, were all part of a nefarious scheme to take him down. That is, there was an ongoing plot stretching from the investigation into ties between Russia and his 2016 campaign to the two prosecutions overseen by the special counsel Jack Smith into his mishandling of classified documents and efforts to overturn the 2020 election.

To date, Mr. diGenova and others involved in the case have found it difficult, and time-consuming, to meet the standards of evidence and jurisdiction needed to prove anything close to a conspiracy in a court of law.

Still, the pressure has not relented. The dozen prosecutors still pursuing the inquiry are fast-tracking narrower cases against some chief targets that could be brought quickly, according to people briefed on their work. Leadership of the effort has defaulted back to Washington, and is now being directly overseen by one of Mr. Blanche’s top deputies, Aakash Singh, those people said.

A Justice Department official said leaders in Washington had “full confidence” in the prosecutors now working on the case and would act to uphold the law should “evidence of misconduct present itself.”

Even if charges are never filed, Mr. Trump has already instilled fear in — and imposed steep financial costs on — potential targets, in his view giving them a taste of what he experienced when he was under investigation.

Two targets have borne a particular brunt: James B. Comey, the former F.B.I. director fired by Mr. Trump in the early stages of the Russia inquiry, and John O. Brennan, the former C.I.A. director who played a role in instigating that investigation.

Inside the Justice Department, another price is being paid.

The investigation has upended the U.S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of Florida, one of the most important in the country, which has been plagued by staff departures and low morale under its Trump-appointed leader, Jason A. Reding Quiñones, according to current and former prosecutors. The problems with the grand conspiracy case have exacerbated what officials in Washington have described as a growing lack of confidence in Mr. Reding Quiñones by his superiors.

The office once had more than 200 lawyers. It is now slightly more than half that size, after a spate of firings and resignations.

Prosecutors have watched the case play out with embarrassment and horror. Many have been so unwilling to join the investigation that Mr. Reding Quiñones, an Army reservist, was forced to bring in military lawyers to backfill the ranks.

The chief of the office’s criminal division has been sidelined. The office’s health care fraud unit has been decimated. Many prosecutors say the office feels leaderless, and are worried that a place once known for big drug and white-collar cases has pivoted to politics.

Even furniture has been repurposed to equip the inquiry’s two work spaces, one on the fifth floor of the main Miami office and the other up the coast in Fort Pierce.

It is not clear who coined the term “grand conspiracy,” or when it became shorthand for the catchall investigation. July 2025 is as good a place to start as any.

That is when John Ratcliffe, the C.I.A. director, issued a criminal referral of Mr. Brennan to the F.B.I., accusing him of lying to Congress about an intelligence assessment in early 2017 that determined Russia had interfered in the 2016 election.

The case was sent to David Metcalf, the Trump-appointed U.S. attorney in Philadelphia, but it quickly stalled as prosecutors struggled to make headway. Career prosecutors threatened to revolt if the office went forward.

By fall, Mr. Blanche, then the department’s second-in-command, plucked the case from Mr. Metcalf and gave it to Mr. Reding Quiñones, who was close to the right-wing influencers clamoring for a wide-ranging prosecution of the president’s opponents.

Loudest among them: Mike Davis, a media-savvy lawyer who has relentlessly promoted the case as the best way to prove that Mr. Trump has been undermined by the establishment from the moment he took office.

Mr. Davis, a former Senate aide adept at hurling social media thunderbolts that catch Mr. Trump’s eye, aimed high. He pushed the idea that the inquiry should expand to include targets like former President Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton.

Mr. Davis was among those arguing to steer the case to Mr. Reding Quiñones in the president’s home state. The move made tactical sense. Prosecutors could avail themselves of a grand jury in the Fort Pierce courthouse where the only sitting judge is Aileen M. Cannon, a Trump appointee who issued several rulings favorable to the president, especially in the classified documents case against him.

Mr. Trump, impatient to see splashy results, cheered and coached from the sidelines, even posting a fake video showing Mr. Obama being arrested in the Oval Office.

But the move to Florida did not translate into immediate success.

One big problem, in the view of Mr. Blanche’s aides, was Mr. Reding Quiñones, whom they viewed as a feckless and inexperienced manager not capable of running the day-to-day operations of his office, let alone the grand conspiracy case.

Moreover, they felt that Mr. Reding Quiñones spent too much time in Washington and too little in Florida. To address that concern, Mr. Singh recently removed him from the attorney general’s advisory committee, which meets at department headquarters, to refocus his energies on Miami, according to two people with knowledge of the move.

But he was hardly the only problem.

By early 2026, the case had landed on the desk of Maria Medetis Long, a respected national security prosecutor in Miami, who approached the inquiry with an open mind. She eventually determined that the evidence did not support indicting Mr. Brennan, according to people familiar with her account. In April, she put her findings in writing. She was suddenly removed from the case.

Since then, the investigation has expanded beyond Mr. Brennan. The flurry of grand jury subpoenas issued since last year, hailed as bombshells by Trump-friendly news outlets, hints at its breadth.

Prosecutors have demanded documents from other officials connected to the Russia investigation, including James R. Clapper Jr., the former director of national intelligence; Andrew G. McCabe, the former deputy director of the F.B.I.; Peter Strzok, a former F.B.I. counterintelligence agent; and Lisa Page, a former lawyer at the bureau.

They have also issued subpoenas demanding testimony from Daniel C. Richman, who is a longtime confidant of Mr. Comey’s, and several F.B.I. agents who took part in the August 2022 search of Mar-a-Lago, Mr. Trump’s Palm Beach club and residence, a key investigative step in the classified documents case.

The prosecutors also want testimony from Mr. Brennan. But amid the recent turmoil, they pushed back his appearance from its initial date on Oct. 15 to at least early December.

Enter Mr. diGenova, who as U.S. attorney in Washington four decades ago led investigations of the Israeli spy Jonathan Pollard and Marion Barry, the city’s mayor.

He was a familiar presence in the capital, known as one of the more dulcet crooners to perform in musical skits at the annual Gridiron Club dinner.

But in recent years, Mr. diGenova has established himself as a stalwart and aggressive Trump defender who embraced unsubstantiated claims about the 2020 election championed by his close friend Rudolph W. Giuliani.

In early 2025, with the help of Mr. Davis, he secured an assignment in Miami as the head of that office’s civil rights division, where he intended to investigate Mr. Trump’s adversaries.

But Pam Bondi, the attorney general at the time, vetoed his hiring, according to two former department officials. Department officials thought he was too old for such a demanding job when his name came up a year later. Ms. Bondi, on the verge of being fired, argued that he had not been in a courtroom for many years.

Mr. Trump, then 79, thought otherwise.

He instructed Susie Wiles, his chief of staff, and Mr. Blanche to sign him on.

Mr. diGenova showed up for his first day at work with a 190-page memo on how to proceed, listing more than 50 “overt acts” in the conspiracy he wanted to investigate. They started with what he saw as the original deep-state sin — a December 2016 meeting in the White House that he believed to be the linchpin of the conspiracy against Mr. Trump.

At that meeting, Mr. Obama and his aides authorized the intelligence assessment that eventually showed Russia had interfered in the election Mr. Trump had just won. The participants have denied that anything illegal took place.

One of Mr. diGenova’s first moves reflected an understanding of the daunting challenges of proving his theory. He asked his predecessor, Ms. Medetis Long, to rejoin the investigation. She turned him down, according to the people familiar with her account. He also made it known that he was looking for cooperating witnesses among the targets of the inquiry, even though Mr. Brennan and Mr. Comey were unlikely to help him.

By May, he had begun hiring staff, including his wife, Victoria Toensing. He immediately encountered problems securing volunteers from either Miami or Washington.

Few career agents or attorneys wanted anything to do with it. As of now, most of the prosecutors on the team are military lawyers or were dispatched from other offices.

Among those who signed on: An F.B.I. agent who had investigated a conspiracy theory that the 2020 election had been hacked by Italian satellites and who was part of a special team assembled by Kash Patel, the bureau’s director. There were a largely unknown prosecutor from Fargo, N.D., and a Stanford law professor best known for having written memos justifying the use of torture during the global war on terrorism.

There was a young Justice Department official sent to Florida from Washington who had served as a clerk to Judge Cannon. And then there was Mr. Olsen, a longtime election denier who had no experience in working on criminal cases.

The case that Mr. diGenova hoped to build involved a wide array of targets — not only Mr. Brennan, Mr. Comey and others from the Russia inquiry, but also the prosecutors led by Mr. Smith, the special counsel.

He quickly confronted hurdles. The first: Any crimes arising from the Russia investigation, which ended in 2019, already fell outside the five-year statute of limitations, and had no obvious connection to South Florida. Other problems emerged.

Just as Mr. diGenova was settling in, Jack Eckenrode, an F.B.I. veteran best known for having gone after Mr. Brennan and Mr. Comey during the Russia inquiry, questioned a central premise of the investigation — that the court-approved search of Mr. Trump’s residence was a politically motivated intrusion that tainted everything that followed.

Mr. Eckenrode, part of a special squad assembled by F.B.I. leaders, told Mr. diGenova that Judge Cannon had already ruled that the search of Mar-a-Lago was lawful. That finding, he said, made it difficult to use the search as evidence of a conspiracy connecting Washington to Florida, according to people briefed on the exchange.

Mr. diGenova disagreed — he thought that point was legally irrelevant — and he called Mr. Patel, who pulled Mr. Eckenrode off the case, one of those people said.

By this time, Mr. diGenova was also becoming frustrated with the resources given to his inquiry. There were never enough lawyers, he told Washington, and the ones he had were so young that he had to block off time to teach them the basics, like grand jury presentations.

In late summer, Mr. Reding Quiñones agreed to set aside $1 million from the office’s allocated budget to build a secure facility in Fort Pierce to review classified materials.

Mr. Blanche’s staff rejected the idea.

Why waste money? There was already a facility nearby run by the F.B.I., they said, according to people with knowledge of the exchange.

Under the clash of personalities was a deeper divide on how best to move forward.

Mr. diGenova, who wanted to take aim at big-name targets, told one associate he believed that Mr. Blanche was less interested in proving the conspiracy to destroy the president than in securing rapid box-checking indictments of low-level players to keep Mr. Trump happy.

Mr. Blanche, he told that person, was so anxious to maintain his position that he did not want to tell Mr. Trump the truth: A successful investigation needed time.

The attorney general acknowledged the inquiry’s complexities on a podcast earlier this year. “I’m not suggesting that we don’t have that evidence,” he told Sean Hannity of Fox News. “I’m saying when you talk about the challenges, that’s the challenge.”

Mr. Blanche had his own complaints. His team thought Mr. diGenova was too scattered, too combative and too slow, according to three current and former officials. It did not help that around this time Mr. diGenova and Ms. Toensing left for a long-planned vacation to France.

By early September, Mr. Blanche dispatched two prosecutors from Washington to Florida to move things forward. During a heated meeting, they peppered Mr. diGenova’s staff with questions about its work before the grand jury.

The coda came when members of Mr. diGenova’s team offered him a readout of their closed-door meeting with the two prosecutors: Washington would now be running things.

Mr. diGenova, infuriated, said he would instruct U.S. marshals to remove the prosecutors from the grand jury room if they showed up there to interfere, the officials said.

Mr. Blanche responded with a profanity-laced phone call and summoned Mr. diGenova to Washington. The attorney general wanted to recount his grievances in person, but never actually planned to fire Mr. diGenova, according to a person close to Mr. Blanche.

He never got that chance.

item.title: Inside Ken Paxton’s Private Testimony About His Money
item.description:
Ken Paxton sat for hours in a federal building in Fort Worth as government lawyers grilled him under oath about his growing wealth and questionable investing history.

At the time, in December 2014, Mr. Paxton was a fast-rising Republican star. He had just been elected the next attorney general of Texas. But outside of public view, he was under scrutiny as part of a federal investigation into possible fraud.

The deposition in the case, obtained by The New York Times, was one of the earliest episodes in what would become a decade-long pattern for Mr. Paxton: accusations of corruption and other illegal conduct repeatedly emerged, only to be resolved without a conviction.

Now, as Mr. Paxton is locked in a fierce Senate race in Texas, the deposition offers a previously unseen account of his finances, his attitude toward money and how he used his connections within the State Legislature to amass his wealth.

Since his first election to public office in 2002, Mr. Paxton has grown his wealth through business investments and real estate purchases into a personal fortune with a reported value of up to $23 million. His assets now include multiple mutual funds, a cellphone tower and 15 properties across six states.

Mr. Paxton has rarely answered questions publicly about how he accumulated this wealth on a government salary. His finances have been the subject of repeated investigations by local, state and federal authorities into alleged bribery, fraud and self-dealing. The issue has been a frequent line of attack from his political opponents, including James Talarico, the Democratic state lawmaker running against him for Senate.

The 2014 deposition was part of a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission investigation into Servergy Inc., a technology start-up based in McKinney, Texas, which is part of the district that Mr. Paxton represented as a state lawmaker. The start-up’s founder, William Mapp III, known as Bill, was accused of making false claims to investors.

The S.E.C.’s lawyers wanted to know whether Mr. Paxton hid that he had received compensation for recruiting investors for the company.

The S.E.C. eventually brought civil fraud charges against Mr. Paxton that were dismissed. In addition to the federal inquiry, Mr. Paxton was indicted by a grand jury on state securities fraud charges in 2015. In 2024, he reached a deal to avoid trial while admitting no wrongdoing.

Under oath in 2014, Mr. Paxton told the federal lawyers that he had invested more than $400,000 in various companies. But between legislating and campaigning, he said he didn’t have time to track his investments. In fact, Mr. Paxton said, he could not locate stock certificates potentially worth $200,000.

“I’m so busy,” he said in the deposition, “I don’t always keep track of this kind of stuff.”

The deposition also shed more light on how he defended himself against the securities fraud allegations, which he spent the next decade fighting. Mr. Paxton used phrases like “I don’t remember” or “I don’t recall” more than 200 times when addressing questions. He also tried to deflect to other men he invested with and to his wife, Angela.

“I haven’t prepared a tax return in a long time because I don’t have time, so typically — actually my wife actually does them,” Mr. Paxton said, when asked about a line in his tax returns that seemed to contradict part of his testimony.

Nick Maddux, a senior adviser to Mr. Paxton, said the release of the deposition was meant to distract from the election and Mr. Paxton’s opponent.

“This is a 12-year-old deposition about a case that ended without a conviction, handed to the press by a political opponent less than a month before Election Day,” Mr. Maddux said. “Like President Trump, the attorney general has been politically persecuted for years for standing up to the establishment, and Texans have seen through it every time.”

The Times obtained the December 2014 deposition from a person who opposes Mr. Paxton’s election to the Senate. The Times independently confirmed its authenticity.

Mr. Paxton has been questioned under oath at least three times in the past decade, but none of the depositions were public.

The Talarico campaign has sought the release of two depositions that Mr. Paxton gave in a different case. A lawyer representing Mr. Paxton’s wealth manager is fighting to keep them sealed.

Mr. Paxton’s recounting of the Servergy transaction began at a Dairy Queen in McKinney. In the deposition, he said he intended to invest $100,000 in Servergy and met Mr. Mapp there to give him a check. Mr. Mapp turned down the money, Mr. Paxton said, and instead gifted him 100,000 shares of stock.

Mr. Paxton attributed Mr. Mapp’s generosity to his religious beliefs.

“I said, Well, who do I make the check out to?” Mr. Paxton told the government lawyers, according to the deposition. “He said, I can’t take your money. God doesn’t want me to take your money.”

The value of the shares eventually grew to $200,000, according to Mr. Mapp’s emails to Mr. Paxton that were described in the deposition.

The government’s lawyers asked why Mr. Mapp, who was actively seeking other investors, would give Mr. Paxton shares for free.

“It was not logical,” Mr. Paxton responded in the deposition, before adding that “Bill is a spiritual person.”

Mr. Paxton said he did not ask a lawyer whether it was “appropriate” to accept the shares.

He listed the shares as stock he held or acquired on his annual financial reports filed with state ethics regulators. Andrew Cates, an expert in Texas ethics laws, said Mr. Paxton may have violated state rules by not also disclosing that the shares were a gift.

Mr. Paxton told the government lawyers that he could not remember the location of the certificate proving he owned the stock. He said he was too busy taking his daughter to visit colleges and preparing to be attorney general.

Mr. Paxton’s testimony provided new insight into what he said was a hands-off approach to investing that helped grow his fortune as a state lawmaker.

Given his busy schedule, Mr. Paxton said he would delegate investment pitches to a member of his legislative staff.

The aide would look at the pitch and decide whether or not to consider it, Mr. Paxton said. Mr. Paxton said he would often run the idea by Byron Cook, a Republican lawmaker in the Texas House at the time who had founded a successful video game company, and other businessmen he knew who invested together.

“That’s been my strategy,” Mr. Paxton said, “rely on other people that know this stuff better than I do.”

At the time of the deposition, Mr. Paxton had investments in more than two dozen different businesses. He discussed a handful of those businesses in his testimony, saying he had invested between $50,000 and $175,000 in each. One investment saw a return of $250,000.

Mr. Paxton would eventually place many of his assets in a blind trust after questions over potential conflicts of interest were raised.

The relationship between Mr. Cook and Mr. Paxton did not last. In 2015, Mr. Cook accused Mr. Paxton of steering him and others into investing in Servergy without disclosing that he had received compensation.

The accusation was part of the criminal indictment in state court. Mr. Paxton reached a deal with prosecutors in 2024 to pay Mr. Cook and another investor about $300,000 in restitution and perform community service. Through a lawyer, Mr. Cook did not respond to requests for comment.

Servergy eventually paid a $200,000 penalty to settle separate federal civil fraud charges unrelated to Mr. Paxton. Mr. Mapp lost his job and has avoided a public profile since then. He could not be reached for comment.

Federal lawyers questioned Mr. Paxton about emails central to their fraud case in which Mr. Mapp appeared to offer him a commission for recruiting new investors. Mr. Paxton said he did not remember reading many of Mr. Mapp’s emails and insisted he did not perform services for the company.

When confronted with a copy of his own tax returns, on which the government’s lawyers said Mr. Paxton had disclosed $100,000 for “legal services” to Servergy, Mr. Paxton directed the lawyers to his wife, who he said prepared the form.

Now a state senator, Mrs. Paxton filed for divorce in 2025, accusing Mr. Paxton of adultery. She declined to comment for this article.

A federal judge dismissed the S.E.C.’s fraud case against Mr. Paxton in 2017, ruling that he was under no obligation to tell investors that he had received something of value from Mr. Mapp.

Mr. Paxton said in the deposition that he never had reason to doubt Mr. Mapp’s statements that the company would be successful.

“I tend to trust people until they prove otherwise,” Mr. Paxton said. “Once they lie, then you have got a whole different issue. That’s what’s so difficult about people not telling the truth.”

item.title: Why This Election Could Be More Complicated for Democrats Than Polls Suggest
item.description:
The party out of power typically makes gains in midterm elections. With President Trump unpopular and gas prices stubbornly high, both parties expect Democrats to win seats.

Will it be a blue wave, though? And if so, will it be strong enough to flip both chambers of Congress? Not all waves have the same gravitational force.

In 2006, when President George W. Bush and Republicans faced a backlash over the Iraq War, Democrats flipped 31 seats in the House and five in the Senate, winning both chambers. Mr. Bush called it a “thumpin’.”

In 2018, in Mr. Trump’s first term, the wave was even larger in House races, with Democrats flipping 41 seats. They failed to win control of the Senate, however, and actually lost two seats to Republicans.

Signs are now piling up that another Democratic wave may be coming. Many officials in both parties privately say that they expect Democrats to win back the House, and that the main question is how many seats will change hands. The Senate, long seen as easier for Republicans to hold, now appears to be a tossup. Polls suggest that the party is playing defense even in states Mr. Trump won by double digits two years ago.

Election forecasting is a dangerous business — Republican fortunes could still turn around — but history is often a useful guide. That is why officials in both parties wonder if these midterms will look like 2006, when Democrats flipped both chambers, or 2018, when Republicans were wiped out in House races but picked up two seats in the Senate.

“All these races that are showing we’ve got a two- or three-point lead or it’s a tossup, we could end up losing all of them by two points,” former President Barack Obama said on Wednesday at a fund-raiser for Senate Democrats. “It’s within the margin of error.”

Democrats currently face challenges that did not exist in those earlier midterms. Republican redistricting gains have narrowed the House battleground. The party also has a significant cash advantage. Most of this year’s battleground Senate races are in states Mr. Trump won easily in 2024. The country has only grown more polarized. And the Democratic Party’s brand remains diminished, with liberal voters mistrustful of its leaders.

“The fact that Democrats allowed Donald Trump to get elected twice is nuts,” said Representative Jason Crow of Colorado, a Democrat who was first elected in 2018. “We have more on our plate and more to do and more to prove now than we had in 2018.”

Some Republicans, for their part, worry that their messaging this year may not be as effective as it was in 2018.

“Trump is the larger-than-life character in this election,” said former Representative Steve Stivers of Ohio, who led House Republicans’ campaign committee in 2018. “There’s no Nancy Pelosi on the Democratic side. There are folks trying to use A.O.C. and the D.S.A., but I’m not sure it has the same knowledge with voters.”

The Iraq War dragged down Mr. Bush in 2006, and Mr. Trump faced a mass defection of educated suburbanites from his party in 2018. But both years, Americans felt fairly confident about the economy.

That is not the case now.

With gas prices and interest rates up, inflation stubbornly refusing to yield and Mr. Trump’s tariffs causing a surge in prices in rural America, the country appears to be seriously angry about the cost of living.

The University of Michigan’s Index of Consumer Sentiment is down 33 percent since Mr. Trump returned to office in early 2025. In May, the index reached its lowest point since it began tracking monthly data in 1952.

“In 2018, people weren’t that sour on the economy,” said former Senator Heidi Heitkamp of North Dakota, a Democrat who lost her re-election bid that year as rural states turned hard toward Republicans. “They were shocked by the craziness, but they felt pretty good about the economy before the pandemic.”

Mr. Trump, she added, “still had much more good will than he has right now.”

Eight years ago, furious online donors powered a Democratic fund-raising surge that Republicans could not match.

Now Republicans have built a huge financial edge that has left Democrats begging for help.

The Democratic National Committee is effectively broke. The party’s House and Senate committees and their allied super PACs trail far behind Republicans in fund-raising. And Mr. Trump’s enormously powerful super PAC, funded in part by business executives and corporations looking to curry favor with his administration, has given his party an extra advantage.

The disparity between the parties is perhaps most acute in Texas.

Republican super PACs have directed more than $150 million to help their Senate nominee, Ken Paxton. Democratic super PACs have invested just $4 million so far for their party’s nominee, James Talarico, who has spent more than $60 million of his campaign’s money.

In just about every midterm election, candidates from the president’s party try to avoid national headwinds by making their elections about local issues.

It rarely works.

Congressional incumbents who have lost in past wave elections compared the experience to struggling through quicksand. Try as they might to dig themselves out from the downward pull of an unpopular president — as some Republicans have recently done by voicing opposition to the war with Iran or questioning immigration raids — the effort is usually futile.

“You can do everything right and if the environment is against you, you’re not going to win,” said former Representative Chris Chocola of Indiana, a Republican who lost his seat in the 2006 Democratic wave. “You’re not just swimming upstream, you’re almost drowning. There’s not much you can do to extract yourself.”

Only one of the Senate seats Democrats are trying to flip is in a state, Maine, that former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024. The rest — in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas — are in states Mr. Trump carried all three times he has run for president.

Former Senator Claire McCaskill of Missouri, a Democrat who lost in 2018, said her state had shifted toward Mr. Trump in 2016 in ways she could not arrest two years later.

“I’ll never forget — in 2016, I was seeing flags and bumper stickers and handmade signs saying, ‘I’m a deplorable,’” Ms. McCaskill said. “I remember just thinking, ‘This is different, I haven’t seen this.’ People were anxious to claim him as their guy, and that was still there in 2018.”

Mr. Trump has sought to rekindle that connection with Republican voters by telling them to pretend he is on the ballot this year.

In 2018, most Democrats did not make Mr. Trump the centerpiece of their campaigns. They ran instead on health care, attacking Republicans for a failed attempt to repeal the Affordable Care Act and for cutting taxes for the wealthy.

This time, the president has far less good will with voters and has done little to convey that he is concerned about their day-to-day economic concerns.

“Trump was the background music last time, and now he’s much more in the foreground,” said Howard Wolfson, a political aide to Michael R. Bloomberg, the former New York mayor who directed $112 million to back Democrats in 2018. “You’re seeing more Democratic candidates attempting to tie their opponents to Trump because his numbers are much worse.”

One such Democrat is Roy Cooper, who is leading polls of the Senate race in North Carolina. He released a video last week criticizing his Republican rival, Michael Whatley, for being a Trump acolyte.

Mr. Cooper said that his opponent was “pretty much going to do and say whatever this president tells him to do and say, regardless of whether it’s good for the people of North Carolina.”

Twenty years ago, Mr. Bush was forced to campaign in deeply Republican districts because he would not be helpful to his party’s candidates in political battlegrounds.

Two days before the 2006 elections, Mr. Bush traveled to Grand Island, Neb., where he sought to motivate rural Republicans to vote in a suddenly competitive House district by celebrating Saddam Hussein’s conviction and death sentence by an Iraqi tribunal.

Mr. Trump went to Grand Island on Monday for a rally for Senator Pete Ricketts, a Republican whose seat had been considered safe. Mr. Trump won Nebraska by 20 percentage points two years ago.

Last week, the president rallied in Oklahoma, where he won by 34 points in 2024.

The president’s visits, combined with Republican advertising spending meant to shore up incumbent senators in Kansas and South Carolina, suggest that the political battleground has shifted from traditionally purple states to red ones.

For Republicans like Mr. Ricketts and Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas, who had expected to cruise to re-election but were now in competitive races, the political whiplash can be severe and put their campaigning skills to the test.

“In 2018, you had people whose districts that were not competitive suddenly becoming competitive,” said Matt Gorman, who was a senior aide on House Republicans’ campaign committee that year. “In a span of a year, they had to go from sitting in a ruby-red district to sitting in a purple district, and that is hard for some people to do.”

item.title: F.B.I. Arrests Key Suspect in ShinyHunters Hack of Its Own Agents’ Data
item.description:
The F.B.I. has arrested a man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of carrying out the computer hack that stole sensitive information about thousands of F.B.I. employees, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The theft of reams of personal data last month by a criminal hacking group left the nation’s premier law enforcement agency racing to respond as both the investigators and the victims of one of the worst breaches of government data in recent years.

The arrested man is a Canadian citizen and considered to be a primary co-conspirator in carrying out the intrusion, the people said.

Kash Patel, the F.B.I. director, confirmed on Friday that an arrest had been made as part of the bureau’s effort to dismantle the international hacking group. “We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate,” he said.

Officials did not immediately release the man’s name or the specific charges against him.

The breach was announced by a hacking group that called itself ShinyHunters, saying it had pilfered intimate details about F.B.I. personnel from the agency’s jobs portal. ShinyHunters threatened more consequences — which many officials and cybersecurity experts interpreted as a plan to release the data publicly — if the F.B.I. did not rescind an advisory warning the public of the group’s cyberattacks, but later backed off.

In the wake of the breach, the F.B.I. vowed to pursue the group’s members, who are believed by security researchers to comprise a loose collective of young English-speaking hackers in several countries across the globe. The group has been active for years and been responsible for some of the most serious corporate data breaches in recent years, often extorting victims for millions of dollars in exchange for promises to not publish stolen private material.

The F.B.I. hack scooped up home addresses, Social Security numbers, sensitive job assignments, details about employees’ family members and more, according to a New York Times analysis of some of the records that was shared by the hacking group. In an internal memo to its workforce after the hack was disclosed late last month, the F.B.I. said it was operating under the assumption that all employees had been compromised in the hack.

Brett Leatherman, the assistant director for the F.B.I.’s cyber division, said this week that a review had determined that the hack was “the result of a security failure of a platform managed by a third-party organization — after a contractor failed to implement a security patch explicitly issued to secure the platform.” That contractor worked for Accenture, Reuters earlier reported.

The bureau has “removed the contractor and taken all necessary steps to both mitigate any further risk and protect our work force,” Mr. Leatherman said, adding that multiple arrests had already been made.

The arrest this week is the latest in a recent string of international law enforcement actions aimed at ShinyHunters. In September, seemingly before the F.B.I. hack, the authorities in the Netherlands arrested a 24-year-old suspected of being affiliated with ShinyHunters, though the group denied knowing him.

ShinyHunters is considered one of the most notorious and capable cybercriminal enterprises in the world. The group is believed to have breached more than 140 organizations and extorted $70 million since last year, Mr. Leatherman said, and has often targeted third-party vendors and cloud-based platforms.

item.title: Ending a Notable Career, Durbin Laments the Decline of Legislating
item.description:
As a junior member of the House 40 years ago, Senator Richard J. Durbin learned a lot about the art of legislating when he improbably defeated the formidable tobacco lobby to win a ban on smoking on airplanes.

As he prepares to leave Congress after five terms in the Senate and seven in the House, Mr. Durbin fears it is becoming a lost art.

“I really miss when we were legislating,” said Mr. Durbin, an Illinois Democrat and old-school lawmaker who had conspicuous success pushing his priorities through amendment fights on the floor. It is a practice the Senate has all but abandoned as leaders of both parties maneuver to avoid politically risky votes for their members.

These days, leaders decide behind closed doors which proposals get a debate and vote, and “you’re lucky” if yours makes the cut, Mr. Durbin lamented. “The reason I passed the most significant bills in my career was because I had a shot on the floor.”

Mr. Durbin, 81, is on track to finish as the longest-serving senator in Illinois history and has been the No. 2 Senate Democrat — the whip — since 2005. He is among the prominent senior members of Congress winding down their careers at the end of the year, a transition that will significantly change the face of the House and Senate.

Joining him in departing are such notable figures as Senator Mitch McConnell, Republican of Kentucky and a former leader, and Representatives Nancy Pelosi of California and Steny H. Hoyer of Maryland, the Democratic former speaker and majority leader, respectively.

As a top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee and its chairman from 2021 to 2025, Mr. Durbin has been in the middle of the judicial confirmation wars that have consumed the Senate. He was also a member of the Senate and House appropriations committees, directing billions of dollars to his state.

It was as a member of the House Appropriations Committee that Mr. Durbin in 1986 began pursuing the airline smoking ban, motivated by the cancer death of his father and his experience being squeezed between two smokers on a plane ride — almost unimaginable today.

The obstacles were significant in an institution where office ashtrays were still a fixture. Nearing committee approval, he found himself needing the vote of Representative Martin Sabo, Democrat of Minnesota and a more senior colleague who could kill his proposal. Mr. Sabo was not inclined to back him, relishing a calming smoke on his flights home.

“I go to him and I say, ‘Marty, can I ask you a question?’ He said, ‘What?’ And I said, ‘How long can you go without a cigarette?’ He said, ‘Two hours.’ I said: ‘Good. This applies to flights of two hours or less.’”

The amendment passed and became landmark law, initiating a domino effect that led to sweeping nationwide restrictions on smoking.

“I had no idea that was the tipping point,” Mr. Durbin said. “Probably changed the country more than I ever imagined.”

Mr. Durbin saw another opening in 2010 but ran into stiff opposition from Wall Street and the banking community when he pushed his proposal to cap the “swipe” fees banks charge merchants for accepting debit cards.

Backers of a major banking overhaul bill resisted Mr. Durbin’s efforts to add his amendment, fearing it could complicate passage. He was forced to muster a supermajority when other proposals had sailed through with a simple majority.

“I was the 24th amendment on the floor,” Mr. Durbin recounted. “I wasn’t on the Banking Committee. They call the roll and I win.”

He is still exulting in the outcome: “Cost Wall Street $8 billion a year.”

Mr. Durbin also forged alliances across the aisle, working with Senator Charles E. Grassley, Republican of Iowa, to pass a sweeping criminal justice overhaul signed into law by President Trump over conservative objections. He worked with Senator Susan Collins, Republican of Maine, on multiple tobacco-related measures, including a move to strip a $50 billion tax break for the industry that was slipped into a bill in 1997.

“I was a brand-new senator, and he had a lot more experience than I did, and we worked together to repeal that,” Ms. Collins recalled about their amendment, which ultimately passed on a 95-to-3 vote. “He’s always been a great partner because he really cares about getting bills across the finish line.”

Yet one major victory has eluded him for decades, and it stings. Mr. Durbin has been unable to pass legislation establishing permanent deportation protection and a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants brought into the country as children — the so-called Dreamers. He has introduced the Dream Act every Congress since 2001. Despite broad public and congressional support for the legislation, it has repeatedly gotten caught up in bigger immigration fights and never been able to pass on its own.

At Mr. Durbin’s urging, President Barack Obama, his former Illinois colleague in the Senate, instituted the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program through executive order in 2012. It led to tens of thousands of qualified immigrants being able to legally attend school and hold down jobs. Today, the program is under assault amid uncertainty in the courts and an immigration crackdown by the Trump administration, which has declared that DACA does not provide protection from deportation. That has resulted in hundreds of recipients being detained, and some deported.

Stymied legislatively, Mr. Durbin has instead taken the floor to recount the stories of individual Dreamers, their accomplishments and setbacks. His 153rd story, complete with the usual poster-size photograph, was delivered late last month.

It was the account of Karen Montes Gaga, a DACA recipient who received bachelor’s and master’s degrees in education and was an elementary schoolteacher for almost a decade. But the Trump administration was slow to renew her work permit, he said, and she had to leave her classroom in the middle of the school year.

Mr. Durbin challenged the wisdom of penalizing a “teacher who is committed to instilling strong values and work ethic into her students.”

“To my Republican colleagues, I ask you: If you went out looking for the ‘worst of the worst,’ would you choose Karen?” Mr. Durbin said on the Senate floor. “If you want to remove from the United States rapists, murders, terrorists, child predators, would you identify Karen as one of those people? Of course not.”

Mr. Durbin said he takes some comfort from the way spectators in the gallery and Senate pages pay rapt attention as he unspools the backgrounds of DACA recipients.

“All I can do to pass this bill in the closing months is keep telling their stories,” Mr. Durbin said. “If there is anything that emotionally affects me, it is because I’ve come to know these kids, now adults, and what their lives are like.”

“I will tell you,” he added, “I regret not getting that done before I left.”

item.title: Top Democratic Group Pumps Millions Into Kansas Senate Race
item.description:
The top super PAC for Senate Democrats is reserving $5 million in advertisements in Kansas’ newly competitive Senate race, signaling that the party sees a serious chance of winning a red state that once seemed out of reach.

The group, Senate Majority PAC, will spend the money on television spots and digital ads through Election Day, an investment to help narrow the gap between Republican and Democratic spending in the state. The top super PAC for Senate Republicans recently diverted millions of dollars to Kansas to defend its incumbent, Senator Roger Marshall, instead of spending in other states long seen as the main battlegrounds, like North Carolina. It is the group’s first foray into Kansas this cycle.

The move, which has not previously been reported, comes as polls show an increasingly close race between Mr. Marshall and Adam Hamilton, his Democratic challenger. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report moved its rating for the Kansas Senate race from “Lean Republican” to a tossup on Tuesday, and a New York Times/Siena University poll over the weekend showed Mr. Marshall and Mr. Hamilton in a dead heat.

Democrats are now stepping up their efforts in Kansas as they try to win back a majority in the upper chamber.

“The gap is closing in Kansas,” Lauren French, a spokeswoman for the Democratic super PAC, said in a statement.

item.description:
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York is planning to campaign next week in Michigan, where she will join Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate, on a bus tour across the Upper Peninsula and hold rallies of her own in and around Detroit.

The Michigan Senate race is crucial to both parties’ hopes of winning a majority. Dr. El-Sayed is running against former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican who only narrowly lost a Senate race in the state in 2024.

Dr. El-Sayed and Ms. Ocasio-Cortez are planning to visit several towns Thursday in the Upper Peninsula, with scheduled stops in Escanaba, Iron Mountain and Marquette as part of the El-Sayed campaign’s “Shouldn’t Be This Hard” tour.
