item.title: The Midterm Senate Fight Spreads to a Surprising New Battleground
item.description:
Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. The Republican domination of the state’s two Senate seats, lasting nearly a century, is one of the longest partisan winning streaks in Senate history.

But suddenly, a megachurch pastor who became a Democrat this spring appears to have a shot at breaking it.

A race that once barely registered nationally has emerged as one of the most unexpected battlegrounds on a midterm map that has rapidly expanded into longtime Republican strongholds. The arrival of the pastor, Adam Hamilton, as a serious Senate contender in Kansas has come so fast, it appears to have caught the incumbent Republican, Senator Roger Marshall, by surprise.

Polls suggest that the race is neck and neck. This week, the Cook Political Report, a political forecaster, declared the contest a “tossup.” And national Republicans who once hoped that red-state incumbents would look after themselves have promised $14 million to save the seat.

National Democrats are now entering the fray, too. Senate Majority PAC, the top super PAC for Senate Democrats, on Friday revealed plans to spend $5 million in the race.

The pairing of an unconventional challenger — one who was a registered Republican until February — and an embattled incumbent has tantalized Democrats, who believe they just might be able to notch an upset in a state where economic headwinds are hitting particularly hard.

Republicans believe they can muscle through — as long as their base turns out.

“Money won’t be an issue,” said Rob Fillion, the executive director of the Kansas Republican Party. “It’s whether or not Republicans show up to the booths.”

In public, Republicans have worked to project confidence about Mr. Marshall, 66, an obstetrician-gynecologist and a former congressman who dashed Democratic hopes of a surprise flip when he first won his seat in 2020.

In private, though, some Republicans in Washington and Kansas are frustrated that he has not mounted a more robust or nimble response to his challenger in a souring political climate. He has raised just $2.5 million in individual campaign contributions, compared with more than $4 million for Mr. Hamilton.

Voters in Kansas enthusiastically backed President Trump all three times he was on the ballot here, but the deeply agricultural state has been buffeted this year by a series of problems exacerbated by his administration.

The Iran War pushed the cost of diesel fuel to a record high of $6.52 per gallon in September, driving up the costs of shipping and operating farm equipment. (In Kansas, the average price of a gallon of diesel now hovers at just under $6.)

Kansas cattle ranchers were incensed by a Trump administration plan to lower the price of beef by dropping import tariffs. And they pushed back last month when highly visible immigration enforcement raids disrupted the cattle harvest by keeping workers at home.

“Our members want to be left alone,” said Matt Teagarden, the chief executive of the Kansas Livestock Association. “We don’t look for the government to intervene in our markets.”

In a sign of flagging enthusiasm for Mr. Marshall, the trade group decided to sit out this election after endorsing him in 2020, although Mr. Teagarden declined to explain why.

“We had some concerns in terms of where Senator Marshall is,” Mr. Teagarden said.

The senator, who has attacked Mr. Hamilton as “too woke,” has faced persistent questions about how much time he spends at his Florida home, and how those trips were paid for. He sought to rebut those questions this week by inviting a reporter from The Washington Examiner to his hunting cabin in Kansas (he also told the news outlet that the Florida house had just been sold).

And attack ads against him have pointed to the findings of an investigation by The New York Times that found he had sued hundreds of his patients over unpaid medical bills, leading to the arrests of 81 of them for missing court dates.

“That’s just an absolute lie,” he told reporters this week. “I wouldn’t want anyone to be thrown in jail because of that.”

The chairwoman of the Kansas Democratic Party, Jeanna Repass, learned this year that Mr. Hamilton, who switched his party affiliation from Republican to unaffiliated in February, was considering an independent run for the Senate.

She got in touch with him over text. If he ran, she asked, would he please do it as a Democrat?

He did.

As a candidate, Mr. Hamilton, 62, has sought to pin the blame for Kansas’s economic trouble squarely on Mr. Marshall and his support for Mr. Trump. He has assailed the administration for its cuts to health care and — in a rarer message for a Democrat — its ballooning of the national debt.

“The senator that I’m trying to replace — that I’m hoping to help bless by letting him retire to Florida — is not being a champion for the people of Kansas,” Mr. Hamilton said on Thursday night.

Mr. Hamilton was speaking in front of several hundred people at an ornate theater in Hutchinson, a small city in south-central Kansas that boasts either the world’s longest or second-longest grain elevator, depending on whom you ask.

In a stump speech that unspooled his life story in painstaking detail, he spoke of founding the 24,000-member Church of the Resurrection, the largest United Methodist congregation in the country.

And he levied a particularly Kansan insult at the U.S. Senate, saying that like the characters in “The Wizard of Oz,” it’s missing a brain, a heart and courage.

He is more comfortable talking about scripture than policy. When a woman in the crowd asked how he would fix the health care system, he said he was reading as much as he could about it, rather than offering up “some bogus answer.” In interviews, he has struggled to clearly articulate his position on hot-button issues like artificial intelligence.

But his work in the church has lifted his name recognition. “Adam has a reach through the Methodist Church in corners of the state that I don’t even have county parties in,” said Ms. Repass, the state Democratic chair.

And his willingness to sound conciliatory in a moment when Democrats elsewhere are demanding bombastic fighters appears to be helping him build support, particularly among moderate Democrats and among Republicans disillusioned with Mr. Marshall and Mr. Trump. Two Republican former governors, Bill Graves and Mike Hayden, have endorsed Mr. Hamilton. (The other two living Republican former governors, Sam Brownback and Jeff Colyer, have stayed neutral.)

As she left a campaign event in Lindsborg, Kan., a Swedish American enclave where the local university is affiliated with the Evangelical Lutheran Church, Dianna Dawdy, 81, said she thought she would vote for Mr. Hamilton. A Republican, she said she had voted for Mr. Trump three times.

“A traditional Democrat wouldn’t be having this kind of effect,” said David Kerr, a Republican and a former president of the Kansas State Senate. Mr. Kerr helped organize the event on Thursday night in Hutchinson, where people in the crowd milled around in “Ag for Hamilton” and “Republicans for Hamilton” buttons. It is the first time Mr. Kerr has ever come out so publicly in support of a Democrat.

Democrats in Kansas haven’t won a Senate race in a while, but they have posted other victories in recent years.

The second-term governor, Laura Kelly, is a Democrat. And Democrats in the state celebrated when, after the fall of Roe v. Wade in 2022, Kansas voters handily defeated a referendum on a constitutional amendment that would have said there was no right to abortion in the state.

Last week, a poll by The New York Times and Siena University found the race to be evenly split between Mr. Hamilton and Mr. Marshall.

Republicans believe that their base will lock in as the race enters its final weeks — and that partisanship will ultimately win the day.

“The Democrats this cycle don’t have anything to run for,” said Mr. Fillion, the executive director of the state Republican Party. “They’re simply running against President Trump and using fear mongering.”

David Kensinger, a Republican strategist in Kansas, said the state’s Republican tilt was so strong, it could well outweigh any dip in voter enthusiasm caused by high prices or frustration with the president.

“You could both have the closest Senate race in 50 years,” he said, and Mr. Marshall “gets re-elected.”

item.title: James Talarico’s Absence From the Trail Rattles the Texas Senate Race
item.description:
The last time James Talarico held an in-person campaign event was on Sept. 29, at a fund-raiser in New York City, his second there in two days. A day later he appeared virtually before a Hispanic business group, conducting his talk from a hotel room. He had come down with a cold, he told the audience, which he had intended to speak to in person.

Since then, Mr. Talarico has not done any campaign events — a striking absence from the campaign trail at a time when polls show him in position to be the first Democrat in a generation to win statewide in Texas.

His opponent in the Senate race, Ken Paxton, has been hammering Mr. Talarico over his absence for days, suggesting that Mr. Talarico was hiding some underlying problem that he did not want to divulge. On Wednesday, at a rally with President Trump, Mr. Paxton led the crowd of thousands in a chant: “Where is James Talarico?”

Mr. Talarico’s campaign said that the candidate has been recovering from the flu, and that he would return to the campaign trail this weekend. A spokesman for the campaign, JT Ennis, said that Mr. Talarico had held “more than 100 public events” and shaken “tens of thousands of hands” before getting sick.

The Talarico campaign has maintained a steady presence on social media and in emails to supporters, masking the candidate’s absence from live events. Still, the lack of participation by Mr. Talarico himself in any public events — or even in any private fund-raisers via video — caused even some of his supporters to worry.

Mr. Paxton and his Republican supporters have reveled in the moment, creating “missing posters” and demanding that Mr. Talarico pose for a photo holding a newspaper with the date visible to prove he is OK.

“Still no proof of life,” Mr. Paxton’s campaign wrote in an email blast on Friday. “Texans are still asking one simple question: Where’s Jimmy?”

During his last public appearance, before the U.S. Hispanic Business Council, Mr. Talarico explained that he was concerned about spreading his illness.

“I was starting to feel under the weather a few days ago,” he told the audience. “Last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas and I was diagnosed with the flu and so I’m running a fever and I’m at my most contagious right now. I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail. And so I want to keep everybody safe and you know, if I was passing on this illness to somebody and got someone’s grandmother or someone’s baby sick, I couldn’t live with myself. So I thought the best thing to do was to put safety first and put everyone’s health first.”

Mr. Talarico has not spoken in public since. Early voting in Texas begins on Oct. 19.

item.title: Why Overanalyzing the Early Vote Can Be Misleading
item.description:
Voting before Election Day has become more and more common in recent years. In 2024, more than 80 million voters took advantage of this option, a majority of the entire turnout.

In the weeks before Election Day, data on which voters have cast an early ballot, either in person or by mail, is a frequent topic of analysis. Is the early electorate older or younger than in past elections? Is it more Democratic or more Republican? Is the election a record for early voting in a certain state?

These analyses can be intriguing, and they come with the authority of being real data from a live election, but there are limits to what early votes can tell us, especially about the outcome of a race. This year, there may be more uncertainty than ever around mail-in voting after President Trump’s attempts to influence the process, one of which resulted in an executive order that was blocked by the Supreme Court.

Even if early voting continues without many changes, it will come with a series of challenges to analyzing the data.

The most common way to assess the partisanship of early voters is by looking at their party registration. That method largely falls apart in the 19 states where party registration is not recorded, including battlegrounds such as Michigan, Texas and Georgia.

In 19 states, voters do not declare a political party when they register to vote.

Source: L2.

The New York Times

Even when party registration is available, it is an imperfect proxy for how people vote. Many Americans registered to vote decades ago and have not updated their registration, so party statistics often lag behind changes in a state’s political makeup. New Hampshire, which has consistently voted Democratic in presidential races, has more registered Republicans than Democrats. In Louisiana, where the Republican candidate has won every presidential election this millennium, registered Democrats outnumbered registered Republicans until this year.

Even if we could know the party registration statistics of the final electorate, including both early and Election Day voters, they would not be a reliable indicator of results. A look at various recent elections in Florida, for example, reveals that ballots cast in early voting favored Democrats in some elections and Republicans in others.

And in both the 2024 presidential and the 2022 U.S. Senate elections, an average of publicly available poll results was closer to the election result than the proportion of Democrats or Republicans who voted across all methods.

Even if we knew whom early voters were going to vote for, it would be challenging to predict election results because early voters differ systematically from Election Day voters.

People who vote early tend to be some of the most highly engaged. Irregular voters, including younger adults, are more likely to wait longer to return their ballots or to cast a ballot on Election Day. This can make it hard to interpret early-vote data in both primary and general elections.

Before the New York City congressional primaries in 2026, prognosticators pointed to the fact that the average age of Democratic voters was older than it was during the 2025 mayoral primary — a troubling sign for candidates endorsed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani. But young voters picked up the pace during the end of the early voting period and came out to vote on Election Day, propelling multiple primary wins for progressive candidates.

Early votes in recent years have tended to favor Democrats over Republicans in general elections. The 2024 presidential election in Pennsylvania provides a stark example: Even though Kamala Harris won the early vote by 31 percentage points, Election Day voters favored Mr. Trump by 15 percentage points. He won the state by two percentage points.

The difference in vote choice between advance and Election Day voters is not the same across states or even across years within the same state. It can depend on who qualifies to vote by mail, whether early in-person voting is offered, how long the early voting process lasts and whether news late in the process favors one candidate.

Trump did better among voters who cast ballots on Election Day, propelling his victory in the state.

Note: Margins are calculated using unrounded vote shares.

Source: Pennsylvania Department of State.

The New York Times

A further challenge to pre-election analyses of early in-person voting comes from the fact that early voting periods last weeks in most states. The composition of the early ballots often shifts throughout this period.

With mail ballots, those returned well before Election Day may not be representative of the total mail-in votes because voters from one party may wait longer to send their ballots. In the 2024 election in New Jersey, for example, registered Democrats made up 66 percent of voters who returned their mail ballots between Sept. 25 and Oct. 1. In the week leading up to Election Day, however, that figure was 49 percent.

The changes over time in partisanship of mail ballots are also not consistent from one state to another. In 2024, while Nevada and Pennsylvania had large shifts in partisanship over time, it remained relatively flat in North Carolina.

Although a few states have had large-scale early voting for decades, most started more recently. In 2000, 26 states required a reason for any form of early voting and just 14 percent of voters nationwide cast their ballots early. Today, all but three states have no-excuse mail or early in-person voting, and 60 percent of votes in 2024 were cast using one of these two methods.

As a result of this change, few past elections can be used as benchmarks against which to compare early-voting trends.

Despite its limits as a predictor of results, early-voting data can still be helpful.

Voting trends from early ballots can provide information about what to expect as votes begin to be reported.

If, for example, early votes in a particular election are overwhelmingly cast by registered Democrats, we can also expect absentee vote reports on election night to favor the Democratic candidate. The New York Times uses lists of voters who have cast early ballots, along with modeling of their likely vote choice, to build estimates of early-vote results that inform the Needle, our election night model.

In states where race calls stretch for days after the election, shifts in the partisanship of mail ballots over time can indicate what to expect in the ballots counted after Election Day. During the California primaries in 2026, for example, the share of ballots returned by registered Democrats climbed in the two weeks before Election Day.

These “late mail” votes, which are counted in the days and weeks after Election Day, can prove decisive in close races. In the primary election for Los Angeles mayor, Spencer Pratt, a Republican and former reality TV star, appeared to be in second place on election night, but Nithya Raman, a progressive Democrat, pulled ahead as more than 200,000 of these Democratic-leaning “late mail” ballots were counted over the next five days.

Early voting is ramping up across the country, and it can be difficult to make sense of the data coming in. Christine and I looked at some of the challenges and pitfalls in interpreting these numbers. What other questions do you have?

item.title: Democrats and Some Republicans Pan Hegseth’s Plan to Air Execution
item.description:
A handful of Republicans in Congress joined Democrats on Friday in criticizing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream the execution of the man responsible for the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, comparing it to the tactics of terrorist organizations, authoritarian governments and fallen empires.

”I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do,” Representative Austin Scott, Republican of Georgia, wrote on social media on Friday morning. “America is better than that.”

Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a Republican who is retiring and increasingly critical of President Trump and his administration, said the decision was “beyond disgusting.” He likened it to the actions of some of the United States’ most brutal adversaries.

“Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America,” he wrote in a social media post.

The criticism came after an announcement by the Pentagon that it would broadcast the execution of Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people and wounded 32 others in a shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. The execution is to be carried out on Dec. 3 by the military’s first firing squad since World War II, and would be its first execution by any method since 1961.

The decision came at a particularly fraught moment for congressional Republicans, who are fighting to preserve their narrow majorities in both chambers just weeks before the midterm elections. Already burdened by voter discontent over the war with Iran and a string of controversies involving Mr. Hegseth, G.O.P. lawmakers have been struggling to distance themselves from his bellicose stance.

Instead, the idea of a livestreamed military execution thrust some of them into another politically uncomfortable debate.

“An execution shouldn’t be a live-streamed spectacle,” Representative Rob Bresnahan Jr., Republican of Pennsylvania and one of his party’s most endangered incumbents, wrote in a social media post. “The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment. Their pain deserves respect, not a public show.”

Senator John Curtis, Republican of Utah, invoked the ancient Roman philosopher Seneca to warn that turning executions into public events risked corrupting society.

“A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment,” he wrote, adding that broadcasting Mr. Hasan’s death “diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent.”

Even Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on the idea, telling reporters on Friday that he was unsure the plan to broadcast the execution was “actually going to happen.” While he emphasized the brutality of Mr. Hasan’s attack, he added that if his execution were ultimately shown “through livestream, I’m not going to be watching.”

Mr. Hasan was convicted and sentenced to death in 2013. Mr. Trump approved his execution this week, clearing the way for the military to carry out the sentence later this year.

Mr. Hegseth, who recommended the firing squad, said the public should be able to witness the execution of Mr. Hasan to understand the consequences of attacking American service members.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” Mr. Hegseth said in an interview with Real America’s Voice, a conservative outlet, aboard the aircraft carrier U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln on Thursday. He said he was advocating for the public execution “because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

Democrats roundly condemned the move. Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, accused Mr. Hegseth of staging a publicity stunt that would give Mr. Hasan the type of martyrdom he sought.

“Livestreaming an execution is a barbaric spectacle,” Mr. Reed said in a statement. “This is a gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters.”

Still, the announcement drew praise from some of the president’s most vocal allies in Congress, including those in the most politically safe Republican territory.

“This is how every Muslim terrorist should be dealt with. We will share the stream live,” Representative Randy Fine, who represents a solidly Republican district in Florida, wrote in a social media post, adding: “Fire away!”

Representative Andy Ogles of Tennessee, who is not standing for re-election after losing his primary in August, shared the interview in which Mr. Hegseth made his announcement and called it “excellent.”

“Public execution is what this terrorist deserves,” he wrote. “We will be watching.”

Democrats raised both philosophical and legal objections.

Representative Adam Smith of Washington, the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, said the decision was “disturbing and makes a mockery of our legal system.”

“There is a reason why we treat the meting out of justice with the seriousness it demands,” he said in a statement. “We are a democratic country and should take the rule of law seriously, not turn it into a spectacle.”

item.title: Vance Says He Would Not Watch Livestreamed Execution
item.description:
Vice President JD Vance said he would not watch a livestream of the planned execution of the 2009 Fort Hood shooter and cast doubt on whether the Pentagon’s plan for a public execution would go forward at all.

“I see these announcements,” Mr. Vance said after casting his ballot for the midterm elections in his home state of Ohio. “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.”

He continued, “Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s through livestream, I’m not going to be watching it.”

Mr. Vance also suggested that the method of the planned execution of Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people and wounded 32 others in the deadliest shooting at an American military base, was distracting from the severity of his crimes. Mr. Hasan is set to be executed by firing squad, the first soldier to be put to death by that method since World War II. The firing squad is a rare method of execution, but one that has been historically used by the military, particularly during wartime.

“This is a guy who committed, in my view, the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11,” Mr. Vance said. “The people that he was meant to treat — the Army soldiers that he was meant to treat for mental illness and other problems — he took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived.”

He continued, “So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people.”

Mr. Vance’s comments struck a markedly different tone from those of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who called the public execution a “no-brainer.”

“It hadn’t been since World War II since we’ve done that,” he told the far-right influencer Jack Posobiec in an interview, apparently referring to the last known military execution by firing squad. “Well, I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win.”

In Congress, Democrats and some G.O.P. lawmakers blasted the plan to stream the execution after Mr. Hegseth and the Pentagon announced it Thursday.

The remarks by Mr. Vance, a convert to Catholicism, came hours after top Catholic leaders in the United States condemned the planned livestream. Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, the leader of America’s Roman Catholic bishops, said the move was “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered.”

Mr. Vance has repeatedly clashed over U.S. policy with church leaders, including Pope Leo XIV, who he said earlier this year should stay out of American affairs.

The Catholic Church opposes all capital punishment under the reasoning that all human life is sacred. This “unconditionally pro-life” stance also undergirds the Catholic Church’s opposition to abortion, which it views as ending a life.

President Trump is a vocal advocate of the death penalty, and his administration has moved to significantly expand its use. The Pentagon said on Monday that Mr. Trump had approved Major Hasan’s execution.

item.title: Donor Says Kimberly Guilfoyle Sought Money From Him to Cover Debt
item.description:
Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., secretly begged a Republican donor to pay her credit card debt while she was waiting to be confirmed as ambassador to Greece, according to an interview with the donor.

The donor, Eric Deters, said that Ms. Guilfoyle had asked him to wire $100,000 to pay off her American Express card just before her Senate confirmation hearing in early July 2025, promising to serve as his “ride or die in Trump world” if he did.

“Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she wrote in what appeared to be a text message. Communications between Mr. Deters and Ms. Guilfoyle were reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal. Mr. Deters provided what appeared to be screenshots of their correspondence to The New York Times.

Mr. Deters sketched out a tawdry tale in which a member of the Trump family’s inner circle promised access to top administration officials as part of a financial arrangement she insisted be kept hidden. The donor wanted to connect with Pam Bondi, then attorney general, and Billy Long, then the Internal Revenue Service commissioner, for business and personal reasons.

“Every secretary you know defense, transportation, treasury commerce IRS commissioner everyone gets right back to me,” she appears to have written the donor in late June 2025, shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing.

The texts suggest that Ms. Guilfoyle warned him to call her on Signal and keep their interactions strictly private. “You’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship,” she wrote, according to one of the screenshots Mr. Deters shared with The Times.

“Eric, I really wish you would stop papering all these things,” another message said. “It’s really dangerous.”

Democrats immediately pounced on the allegations as evidence of a pay-to-play pattern during the second Trump administration. Representative Robert Garcia, a California Democrat and ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, said such influence-peddling “would be a brazen abuse of power.” Representative Madeleine Dean, a Pennsylvania Democrat who sits on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Ms. Guilfoyle should be fired.

A lawyer for Ms. Guilfoyle declined to comment. Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to answer questions on Thursday about the ambassador’s conduct as he wound up a visit to Athens.

“Just because some source told you something,” he said vehemently, does not mean “it’s gospel.”

Mr. Deters, who has hosted annual pro-Trump events in Kentucky, is a firebrand with his own controversies. In the interview, he said he retired as a lawyer in 2013 after facing disciplinary actions in Kentucky and Ohio. He is now battling an adversary’s motion to hold him in civil contempt in an Ohio case.

He said that he supported President Trump’s policies, but not his administration’s “open grifting and enrichment,” which he said Ms. Guilfoyle exemplified.

Mr. Deters said he met Ms. Guilfoyle after he began holding an annual “Patriots Day Freedom Fest” in Kentucky in 2020. He said he paid $300,000 to Ms. Guilfoyle, $200,000 to Donald Trump Jr. and $100,000 to Eric Trump to speak at the events between 2021 and 2024.

He also donated $125,000 to a pro-Trump super PAC in 2022, according to Federal Election Commission records.

His relationship with Ms. Guilfoyle seems to have intensified after she and Donald Trump Jr. ended their engagement in 2024 and the president nominated her to be an ambassador.

At that point, Mr. Deters asked Ms. Guilfoyle to help him resolve an issue with the I.R.S. involving his tax deductions. He also wanted her to influence the Justice Department to extradite from Pakistan a doctor who had been criminally charged in connection with botched spinal surgeries and to investigate the doctor’s medical insurance company. He said in the interview that he was representing patients in litigation over their operations.

He promised Ms. Guilfoyle a million dollars if he got a legal settlement, and if Tucker Carlson invited Mr. Deters on his podcast to talk about the case.

In the early summer of 2025, as Ms. Guilfoyle’s confirmation hearing neared, he grew increasingly frustrated with what he saw as a lack of results. He claimed that she never broke through with either Ms. Bondi or Mr. Long.

She insisted that she had pulled out all the stops. “I have never worked harder in my life than to promote and protect you,” the texts indicate that she wrote.

She shared with him a copy of a message she said she had sent to Mr. Long, asking him to look into Mr. Deters’s situation. “Don Jr. and I are very close with Eric Deters,” that message reads.

On June 25, 2025, the texts indicate she wrote Mr. Deters: “Please call IRS commissioner Billy Long wrote me back. BOOM.”

Two days later, the texts indicate that Ms. Guilfoyle said Ms. Bondi was the only cabinet member who did not respond immediately to her — even though she claimed that “we are tight.”

Earlier that month, the texts suggest that Ms. Guilfoyle had asked Mr. Deters for backdated invoices. He sent her a letter on June 11 proposing to pay her $50,000 on July 1 — an amount he wrote that he owed — followed by $50,000 on August 1.

“At the time, I’m her friend, I was considering doing it,” he said in the interview. He described the letter as “bs,” saying she wanted it to disguise their arrangement.

On July 3, six days before her confirmation hearing, Ms. Guilfoyle sent an urgent plea for money, a text indicates. “Banks are closed tomorrow,” she wrote with a praying emoji.

“You could just send it here. It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express that’s all that will show,” she said in the text exchange. She included a PDF with American Express instructions, adding that he would be her “special guest” at her confirmation hearing the following week.

He turned her down, saying his wife would divorce him if he paid.

“Your needing $100,000 urgent unfortunately is not going to work,” he wrote. “I wish you luck.”
